title: Goyal calls Egypt India's gateway to Africa: what that means for exporters
subtitle: In Cairo on 15 November, the commerce minister said Egypt can link Indian makers to Africa, as two-way trade hit US$6.5 billion in 2025-26.
content_html:
Picture a shop that sells to one street, then finds a back door that opens onto a whole market. On Sunday, 15 November 2026, in Cairo, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said "Egypt will become the gateway to Africa" for India. He was on a two-day visit with a 132-member business group, The Economic Times reported. He also said the two economies are not rivals and in fact fit together.

So what does a "gateway" really mean for an Indian trader? And how big is this trade today? Here is the simple version.

How much do India and Egypt trade?

India and Egypt traded goods worth US$6.5 billion in the year 2025-26 (April 2025 to March 2026), says the page of India's mission in Cairo. Of that, India sold Egypt goods worth US$3.87 billion, and bought goods worth US$2.60 billion.

Think of two friends who swap snacks at school. India gave more than it took: about $1.27 billion more. That gap is called a trade surplus, which means a country sells more to a partner than it buys from it.

The trade is also growing fast this year. From April to September 2026, trade between the two countries stood at US$5.04 billion, up 64% on the same six months a year before, the commerce ministry said ahead of the visit.

At an event for the Indian community in Egypt, Goyal called the US$6.5 billion figure a start: "the sky's the limit", he said.

What does India sell, and what does it buy?

India's main sales to Egypt are petroleum products, engineering goods, chemicals, cotton yarn, buffalo meat and medicines, India's mission in Cairo lists. From Egypt, India mainly buys petroleum products, inorganic chemicals, mineral compounds and citrus fruits.

The commerce ministry's own list, reported by The Economic Times, adds crude oil, fertilisers and cotton to what India buys. India is the fifth largest seller of goods to Egypt, the mission says.

One small rule change shows how this trade works day to day. Days before the visit, India's foreign trade office gave meat sellers three more months to move to a new halal certificate needed for meat going to Egypt. The deadline went from nine months to twelve, so Egyptian checking bodies could finish signing up.

So what is a "gateway"?

Imagine a samosa seller in a busy railway station. Crowds from every train walk by, so one stall can reach far more buyers than a stall in a quiet lane. That is the role Goyal described for Egypt.

Before the trip, the Federation of Indian Export Organisations set out the idea. Egypt has a network of free trade agreements covering markets across Africa, the Arab region and parts of Europe, plus easy sea links across the Mediterranean, the group said. A free trade agreement is a deal where countries cut or remove the import tax they charge on each other's goods.

So an Indian company could make or finish a product in Egypt, then sell it to those markets at a lower tax. But there is a catch. The group said this is subject to "rules of origin". These rules decide where a product truly "comes from". A phone just put in a new box in Egypt may not count as Egyptian. One that is really made there may.

Where does the Suez Canal come in?

The Suez Canal is a man-made waterway in Egypt that big ships sail through. Next to it is the Suez Canal Economic Zone, set up in 2015. It covers over 461 square kilometres on both banks of the canal, sits where major shipping routes meet, and aims to pull in factories and foreign money.

Ahead of the trip, the commerce ministry said chances to work together in this zone, along with ports, logistics and manufacturing, would be part of the talks, ET reported.

Money is meant to flow both ways

Indian firms already have a big footprint in Egypt. Over 700 Indian companies are registered there, and about 70 of them are active, with combined investment of more than US$5 billion, says India's mission. These companies give direct and indirect work to about 40,000 Egyptians.

The other direction is tiny. India got only US$11.5 million in foreign direct investment from Egypt between April 2000 and June 2026. That is money a foreign company puts into a business here, like a factory or an office.

That is one reason the visit included a meeting with Ahmed ElSewedy, chief of the Egyptian power and cable group ElSewedy Electric, on 14 November. They talked about working together in electrical equipment, smart meters and data centres, ET reported. The ElSewedy group already has an investment in India in smart electricity meters, according to India's mission in Cairo.

Paying each other is getting simpler too. In June 2026, a special rupee account opened by SBI with Egypt's Banque Misr started working, to help traders settle bills at lower cost.

What this can mean for young Indians

The commerce ministry named manufacturing, medicines, automobiles, textiles, chemicals, engineering goods and food processing among the areas where the two countries can work together more. Goyal said trade "has to be two-way" and "a win-win between the two nations".

For a student thinking of an export career, the lesson is simple. A trade deal on paper is only half the story. Knowing the rules of origin, the certificates a product needs and the right partner country is what turns a "gateway" into real sales.
